Body: Language Quote 1
cells.description: From 2008 Interview with Guy Cools

additional_fields.html-content:
"At first the only way I could think of it was treating it like music, tricking myself into thinking I was playing a percussion piece, which is a trick I sometimes still use. Depending on the performance, the accuracy of the movements comes very much from the musicality: the score is written musically and I am just performing that. The fact that it is bigger movement and does not actually produce sound is immaterial." Matteo Fargion

(from the interview at Sadler's Wells London, 15 December 2008 titled The Musical Body with Guy Cools and published in Body: Language #4)

cells.title: Body: Language Quote 2
cells.description: From 2008 Interview with Guy Cools

additional_fields.html-content:
"I still have the original score of Hands that Matteo wrote. In a way that process of translating, of squeezing movement into musical structures, was already there then." Jonathan Burrows

(from the interview at Sadler's Wells London, 15 December 2008 titled The Musical Body with Guy Cools and published in Body: Language #4)

cells.title: Body: Language Quote 3
cells.description: From 2008 Interview with Guy Cools

additional_fields.html-content:
"There was a certain point when I thought that a lot of the dance that I was seeing and experiencing, apart from ballet, had let go of pulse. I understood that this was perhaps to do with the dance needing to assert itself as an art form in its own right, because for many years it was seen as a sister art form to music." Jonathan Burrows

(from the interview at Sadler's Wells London, 15 December 2008 titled The Musical Body with Guy Cools and published in Body: Language #4)

additional_fields.html-content: It was never the intention, the big idea, let’s perform something with scores. It was really a necessity. Let’s write that down and then we had no idea how we would present this. Then somebody suggested, well, just read the books and so we gave ourselves that permission. MF, Interview, London 13 September 2013

cells.title: On use of scores in their work
cells.description: Use this cell to put HTML content into a set

additional_fields.html-content: The other thing about a score which is outside of you, your physicality and neurology and so forth is that it tends towards encouraging you away from the habitual patterns and responses and at the same time, paradoxically, because you're not having to negotiate so hard with those habitual physicalities and patterns and responses, in fact in some way you let them be and therefore they're there. JB, Interview, London 13 September 2013

cells.title: Discussion of patterns
cells.description: Use this cell to put HTML content into a set

additional_fields.html-content: The patterns discussed in many of these video recordings including those in the Feldman score, ABBA, the 1,2,3 structure and John Cage's 7, 6, 14, 14, 7 (from Lecture on Nothing) provide structure in the making process, but they are there to be broken, challenged and altered in the context of live performance. The pulse too, a pattern of a sort, is there to be 'rebelled' against. In that sense, the patterns themselves are not interesting, what is more important to Jonathan Burrows and Matteo Fargion are the forms of expression they give rise to. The audience also adds an essential ingredient to the creation of their work as each evening's performance is shaped and changed in the conversation with audience.

additional_fields.html-content:
Generators and Performers

Each time the hands clap a pulse is sent and received by the polygon performer. This pulse triggers one of several possible movements.

This is a short description of some of the mechanics involved. To go beyond the mechanics, as Jonathan and Matteo do, we created several stage scenes for you to look at here. Read some background for this development here.

cells.title: Parallel Worlds
cells.description: Use this cell to put HTML content into a set

additional_fields.html-content: There is nothing in the digital world to match this very live, humanly rich and frail world of the performances of Jonathan and Matteo. But the ideas of linear counterpoint, how the gaps between materials can work, the impact of rhythm and pulse on the senses and the 'dance' that happens in the viewer without thinking when all of these things are in a certain relation is something we could explore. We do this through the creation of a 'stage' where the co-play between generators (patterns) and performers (expressing the patterns) can be watched. This parallel world also has resonances and references (the patterns are coming from a variety of sources) and relations you can explore changing on your own.

In October 2011 at Kaaistudios, Brussels,

eight videos were recorded of Jonathan and Matteo performing fragments from five of their duets. They were then recorded watching and commenting on these short fragments played on the computer. This material was never intended for use on this website, but it proved to be a rich resource giving important insight into aspects of their creative process.
